title: Mean, covariance & transformations
blurb: E, Cov, V and affine maps

hook.title: Converting a price list
hook.text: You sell phone cases at random prices $x$ in AUD. Your supplier gives you a USD list: multiply by 0.65 and add a flat **\$5 shipping**. The *average* USD price moves exactly the same way (scale, then shift). But what about the *spread* of prices? Multiplying by 0.65 squeezes the spread; adding \$5 shipping **slides** everything over without changing the spread at all.
hook.recall: Remember the price list: scaling ($A$) changes both the mean and the spread (the spread by $A\,V\,A^\top$), shifting ($b$) only moves the mean.

explore.intro: Grey = original cloud $x$. Green = transformed cloud $Ax+b$.
tasks: Move $b_1$ and $b_2$ only. Does the covariance reading change?
Set $A$ to $0.5\cdot I$. What happens to the measured variance versus the formula $AV[x]A^\top$?
explore.takeaway: $\mathbb E[Ax+b]=A\mathbb E[x]+b$ and $\mathbb V[Ax+b]=A\mathbb V[x]A^\top$. The formula and the measurement agree: $b$ never appears in the variance.

build.prompt: $x$ has mean 2 and variance 1. Let $y=-3x+1$. **Predict $\mathbb V[y]$** before you reveal.
build.reveal: $\mathbb V[Ax+b]=A\mathbb V[x]A^\top$. In 1-D that is $(-3)^2\cdot 1=9$. The sign flips the cloud but never makes variance negative, and the $+1$ shift disappears. (The mean is $-3\cdot2+1=-5$.)

questions.prompt: For a random vector $x$, which expression gives $\mathbb V[Ax+b]$?
questions.explanation: The shipping fee $b$ shifts all prices equally, so no spread is added. Scaling by $A$ transforms the covariance on both sides.

questions.prompt: $\mathbb E[x]=3$, $\mathbb V[x]=4$ (1-D). Let $y=2x+5$. What is $\mathbb E[y]$?
questions.explanation: $\mathbb E[Ax+b]=A\mathbb E[x]+b=2\cdot3+5=11$. Scale the average, then add the shipping.
$\mathbb V[y]=2^2\cdot4=16$. The $+5$ shipping doesn’t move the spread.
The covariance term vanishes only when $\mathrm{Cov}[x,y]=0$ (e.g. independent variables). Two prices that rise and fall together make the total much more variable than the variances alone suggest.

questions.prompt: A coin: head = 1, tail = 0, and $p(\text{head})=0.7$. What is the mean?
questions.explanation: $\mathbb E[x]=1\cdot0.7+0\cdot0.3=0.7$ (the slide asks this for 0.5 and 0.7).

questions.prompt: $x,y$ are independent, so $\mathrm{Cov}=0$. A student concludes: *“$\mathbb V[x-y]=\mathbb V[x]-\mathbb V[y]$.”* Where is the mistake?
options: Covariance is never zero for independent variables
Variance of a difference is $\mathbb V[x]+\mathbb V[y]-2\mathrm{Cov}[x,y]$, which becomes $\mathbb V[x]+\mathbb V[y]$. Spreads add, even for a difference
The correct answer is $\mathbb V[x]\mathbb V[y]$
questions.explanation: Subtracting an independent noisy price can’t make the result *less* noisy: variances are never negative, so they add. (Squaring the $-1$ in $A\mathbb V A^\top$ again.)
